transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-10
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Michael Torres (CISO, Sapphire), Rina Patel (Cloud Architect), Devon Lee (Head of Platform)

Summary:
This was a security and compliance workshop focused on encryption at rest/in transit, BYOK (bring your own key) workflows, HSM integration, key escrow concerns, and operational key rotation. Customer emphasized strict data residency requirements across EU/US and an internal audit in Q3. Discussed tradeoffs between Redwood hosted KMS, customer-managed cloud KMS, and on-prem HSM. Agreed next steps to share runbooks, SOC2 report, and schedule a hands-on connector test.

Topics: BYOK, HSM connector, key escrow, KMS lifecycle, SOC2/ISO scoping, RBAC/SSO for key ops, audit logs, cross-region residency

Action items (recap at end): see metadata action_items above

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, I'll kick us off. Um, small agenda — BYOK flow, HSM integration options, audit and residency questions, and then next steps.
[00:14] Michael Torres: Thanks Alex. Um, quick note our audit window is mid-September so we need to have the conceptual architecture reviewed and documented by end of July.
[00:21] Rina Patel: Yep, and we'll need the redacted SOC2 reports and the data flow diagrams for legal. Also, we have to make sure key material never leaves EU for certain workloads.
[00:32] Priya Nair: Great, we can cover that. Quick intro on options: Redwood supports three deployment patterns for key management — 1) Redwood-managed KMS with customer key import (we call it hosted BYOK), 2) Customer cloud KMS integration (e.g., CloudProvider KMS + IAM), and 3) On-prem / HSM connector for fully customer-controlled keys.
[00:48] Devon Lee: When you say HSM connector, is that a direct HSM-to-GPU path or is it proxying through a Redwood service?
[00:55] Priya Nair: It's a connector that runs in your VPC — a small service that performs EO (encrypt/decrypt) operations via HSM or Cloud KMS APIs. Traffic is local to your VPC, we don't persist keys. The runtime sends key IDs and ciphertext tokens, the connector [inaudible] performs unwrap/wrap and returns short-lived key material to the inference instance.
[01:12] Michael Torres: Okay, so keys never in Redwood control plane?
[01:16] Alex Chen: Correct for the HSM option. For hosted BYOK, customers upload an encrypted key wrapper using our import API then we store wrapped keys in our KMS substore; we only ever store wrapped keys — cleartext never stored.
[01:28] Rina Patel: I want to be explicit about escrow — our compliance team wants a path to escrow keys for disaster recovery but also strict controls around who can release keys. How do you handle that?
[01:38] Priya Nair: We have two approaches: 1) Key escrow with customer-managed HSM — you replicate a wrapped escrow copy into your HSM cluster, we provide the tooling, or 2) Redwood-managed escrow vault under strict legal / contractual terms, with dual-authorization for key release. But most enterprise customers pick the customer-HSM escrow to avoid third-party custody.
[01:55] Michael Torres: Hmm, our preference is customer escrow in our HSM — we want the audit trail in our systems. Is your connector able to write audit events back to our SIEM?
[02:03] Priya Nair: Yes — connector emits signed audit logs and can push to syslog/CloudWatch/Stackdriver via a sidecar. The logs include operation, key id, requester id, and correlation IDs. We keep a copy (if requested) in Redwood Console for convenience but you can disable that.
[02:19] Devon Lee: Latency — if every inference call requires a key unwrap call to HSM, that kills throughput. How do you avoid that?
[02:26] Priya Nair: Good question. We use short-lived derived data keys and KV cache. The runtime obtains a data-encryption key (DEK) from the HSM once per session or for a prefix and caches it in the GPU host memory (KV cache). So token-level decryption doesn't call HSM per token. We also batch requests; for lower latency paths we suggest a hybrid: a locally cached DEK rotated every N minutes with strict TTLs.
[02:46] Michael Torres: Are you encrypting model weights at rest as well or just request/response?
[02:50] Alex Chen: Both. Model artifacts at rest are encrypted with envelope encryption; model keys are wrapped by the KMS/HSM. Snapshots and cache layers are encrypted, too.
[02:58] Rina Patel: For data residency — we run EU workloads in eu-west region. I need to confirm that any wrapped key material or telemetry won't land in the US. How do you prove that?
[03:07] Priya Nair: For private deployments in your VPC/On-prem, control plane endpoints can be regionalized; we can provide a regional control plane and ensure connectors only talk to eu-west endpoints. We'll also provide an architecture diagram and SLA for data path locality. For hosted customers we have region affinity and strict routing policies, but we'll need to run a dataflow checklist with your infra team.
[03:25] Michael Torres: What's the default lifetime for a DEK if cached locally?
[03:29] Priya Nair: Default is 15 minutes, configurable down to 1 minute. Rotation can be automated with the rotation playbook.
[03:34] Rina Patel: And rotation means rekeying the wrap key in HSM? We need a deterministic rotation and key version mapping for audits.
[03:40] Priya Nair: Exactly — each rotation increments the key version. The connector and runtime tag tokens with key version so you can trace which version encrypted which artifact. We record version in audit logs.
[03:50] Alex Chen: I also wanted to bring up SSO/RBAC for key ops — Redwood integrates with SAML SSO and can map AD groups to granular roles: key_admin, key_operator, read_only_audit. You asked earlier about dual control — that maps to the key_admin role requiring two principals for release.
[04:06] Michael Torres: Do you have examples of role mappings? Our ops team uses Okta + SCIM.
[04:11] Alex Chen: Yes, we have SCIM templates and can share example SAML assertions mapping to roles. We'll include that in the runbook.
[04:18] [00:04:18] Devon Lee: A weird question — if we ever need to rotate to a new HSM vendor, what's the migration path?
[04:22] Priya Nair: We support key export in wrapped form from old HSM to new HSM via a standard rewrap operation. The connector can perform a rewrap job where source HSM unwraps locally and rewraps to destination HSM, all within your network. We also support offline export via export tokens under dual-auth.
[04:38] Michael Torres: Any certifications we should call out? SOC2 Type II, ISO27001 — do you have those?
[04:42] Alex Chen: Yes — Redwood maintains SOC2 Type II and ISO27001; we'll attach the latest reports under NDA. For HSM specifics we provide design documents and operational runbooks.
[04:51] Rina Patel: Audit logs — can Redwood provide immutable logs or do we need to configure our SIEM?
[04:55] Priya Nair: Immutable logs are available if you push them into your own WORM storage via the connector. Redwood's Console has append-only logs but for compliance we recommend pushing to your SIEM/WORM.
[05:04] [00:05:04] Michael Torres: For the BYOK hosted case — who ultimately rotates the wrapping key? If we upload a key, does Redwood rotate it?
[05:11] Alex Chen: For hosted BYOK, the customer controls rotation via API — we will not rotate without your action or explicit authorization. Redwood can automate rotation if you opt in with specific policies.
[05:20] Rina Patel: Can you walk through an example flow end-to-end? From model load, to decryption, inference, and logging?
[05:26] Priya Nair: Sure. Step 1: Model artifact encrypted at rest with envelope key K_model wrapped by K_wrap in HSM. During deployment, runtime requests K_model DEK: the connector performs an unwrap with HSM and returns a short-lived DEK to the runtime over mTLS. Step 2: Runtime caches DEK in GPU host memory, decrypts model tensor chunks into memory for the session. Step 3: Inference uses cached DEK for ephemeral request encryption, if required we encrypt outputs with a per-request key. Step 4: Key usage and operation events are sent to your SIEM and to Redwood Console trace for correlation.
[05:53] [00:05:53] Devon Lee: And where does TLS end-to-end apply?
[05:56] Priya Nair: TLS everywhere — client to API is mTLS, connector to HSM uses HSM vendor's secure channel, internal service-to-service comms are TLS1.3 with mutual auth.
[06:05] Michael Torres: One of our auditors asked about key escrow release policy — can Redwood support a legal escrow release with multi-sig and time lock?
[06:12] Alex Chen: We can support a contractually defined release flow with multi-sig where two named principals approve, and optionally a time lock before release. For customer-managed HSM escrow we hand you the tooling; for Redwood-managed escrow we'll tie release to a legal request process with audit trails.
[06:25] Rina Patel: We also need to ensure continuous attestation of the connector — does Redwood provide a signed integrity report (e.g., image signatures and SBOM)?
[06:33] Priya Nair: Yes — connector images are signed, we publish an SBOM and can produce a signed attestation package for your supply chain checks.
[06:40] [00:06:40] Devon Lee: Any pitfalls customers hit when starting BYOK with you?
[06:44] Alex Chen: Main pitfalls: 1) Not aligning key rotation windows with cached DEK TTLs which cause stale decryption errors; 2) Missing SCIM role mappings which block key ops; 3) Network egress rules — connector needs specific outbound endpoints if you use Redwood control plane. We have a preflight checklist to catch those.
[07:03] Michael Torres: OK can you email that checklist and also sample contract clauses for custody and escrow?
[07:08] Alex Chen: Absolutely — we'll send the runbook, checklist, SOC2 and the SSO mappings after the call.
[07:14] Rina Patel: For the technical follow-up, Priya and I should run a staging test. Priya, can you set up a small PoC?
[07:21] Priya Nair: Yeah I can. I'll spin up the connector in their staging VPC and run unwrap/re-wrap tests. I'll need Rina to grant a temporary HSM test account or simulated HSM credentials.
[07:33] [00:07:33] Devon Lee: One more thing — backup and key escrow durability — what's the recommended replication for escrow copies?
[07:38] Priya Nair: We recommend 3-way replication across your HSM cluster in-region with one geo-replica in another permitted region depending on residency. Replication should be via wrapped tokens, never exporting plaintext.
[07:52] Michael Torres: Are there any charge impacts for HSM operations?
[07:56] Alex Chen: HSM calls are metered — each unwrap/rewrap has a small per-call cost; however, because of DEK caching you won't be charged per inference. We'll include an example cost spreadsheet with projected calls per day.
[08:09] Rina Patel: About SSO/roles — can we force step-up auth for key_admin operations?
[08:14] Alex Chen: Yes, step-up MFA for sensitive roles is supported if your IdP has step-up configured. We can require MFA assertion in the SAML claim for key_admin actions.
[08:24] [00:08:24] Priya Nair: Timecheck — we have about 20 minutes left, do we want to jump into the connector design now or keep this high-level?
[08:29] Michael Torres: Let's do a short design sketch and then end with agreed next steps.
[08:33] Priya Nair: Okay I'll share my screen — here's a simplified diagram (link: https://redwood.example.com/poa/connector-arch) — note: this is a reference, we'll tailor to Sapphire's HSM vendor.
[08:45] [screen shares, some crosstalk]
[09:12] Priya Nair: Diagram notes: connector runs as a k8s deployment in your cluster, it uses a hardware key proxy library to call into HSM. It exposes a local gRPC endpoint to the Redwood runtime over mTLS. Optionally we use sidecars for log forwarding.
[09:30] Rina Patel: That looks fine. What about image assurance? We need signed digests and a simple attestation process for each deployment.
[09:37] Priya Nair: Images are signed; we also support cosign verification in the deployment pipeline. We'll add the SBOM and signing steps to the helm chart.
[09:44] Devon Lee: Any expected downtime during key rotation?
[09:47] Priya Nair: No downtime expected — rotations are versioned; runtime supports seamless switch to new version once components acknowledge. You should coordinate a short maintenance window for dependent services but in practice it's seamless.
[09:59] Michael Torres: Ok, quick compliance question — do you store plaintext model artifacts during snapshotting or backups?
[10:03] Alex Chen: No — snapshots are stored encrypted; backups hold wrapped keys. Restoration goes through the same unwrap flow with your HSM.
[10:11] Rina Patel: About legal — we might want a clause that says Redwood cannot access unwrapped keys without mutual authorization. Do you have standard language?
[10:17] Alex Chen: Yes — we'll include standard BYOK custody clauses and we can work with legal on narrow modifications.
[10:21] [00:10:21] Michael Torres: Any competitors who do this differently we should be aware of?
[10:24] Alex Chen: Some vendors force a single cloud KMS path which reduces control; others require exporting keys to vendor-managed HSMs. Our differentiator is flexible modes and strong observability for audits.
[10:35] Rina Patel: OK let's wrap with next steps and owners.
[10:38] Alex Chen: Recap: Alex to send BYOK runbook, SOC2 report under NDA, connector architecture and preflight checklist. Priya to schedule and run the staging connector PoC with Rina. Rina to provide architecture diagrams and HSM test creds. We'll provision a 2-week dedicated trial for benchmarks.
[10:58] Michael Torres: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[11:02] Alex Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up by EOD tomorrow with the initial artifacts.

End of transcript.
